title: Annotations of Maharatz Chajes on Mishneh Torah, Repentance
heTitle: חידושים ומקורים מהר"ץ חיות על משנה תורה, הלכות תשובה
text: The Keseff Mishneh and the Lechem Mishneh raised a difficulty regarding Maimonides, who says that the scapegoat atones for minor transgressions even without repentance, yet isn't it written, "The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination" (Proverbs 21:27)?

And it appears to me: We say in Tractate Zevachim that a burnt offering (olah) functions as a gift, for if you think it comes for atonement, if the person repented, he is already forgiven the moment he repents; and if he did not repent, "the sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination."

However, since Rambam rules in Chapter 4 of Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot that a burnt offering atones for positive commandments and negative commandments attached to positive commandments (lav hanitak l'aseh), he must hold that the concept "the sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination" does not apply to a mere prohibition of a positive commandment, but only regarding an idolater/apostate (see the Mishneh LaMelech, Chapter 3 of Hilchot Shegagot, Halakha 7, at length). Because of this, Rambam's position here is well-settled.
